title: Evergreen makes invariants part of your code
excerpt: Evergreen lets you write contracts and memory rules that the compiler checks for safety.
body:
Evergreen’s playground shows a tiny program that refuses to compile when a value that must never be zero is created with `0`. The snippet

```rust
type NonZero = usize where self != 0;
impl NonZero {
    fn new(x: usize) -> Self where x != 0 { NonZero(x) }
}
```

fails at the `new` call if the argument is `0`. The page calls this “checked invariants” and highlights that the compiler catches the violation at construction time. The rest of the site explains how the same mechanism powers contracts, memory safety, and proof-level guarantees without adding runtime overhead.

The reader will see how Evergreen embeds preconditions, postconditions, and data invariants directly in the code, how its ownership model tracks live memory, and how proof constructs are erased after verification. A short walkthrough of each feature makes it clear what the language can do in practice.

## Explicit contracts live beside the code

Evergreen treats a `where` clause after a type or function as a contract that the compiler must enforce. In the `NonZero` example the invariant `self != 0` sits next to the type definition, and the constructor adds the precondition `x != 0`. When the compiler processes `NonZero::new(10)` it checks that `10` satisfies the precondition; any other value produces a compile-time error.

A function example from the site demonstrates both a precondition and a postcondition:

```rust
fn increment(n: usize) -> usize where n < usize::MAX ensures result > n { n + 1 }
```

The `where` clause requires the argument to be below `usize::MAX`, and the `ensures` clause demands that the returned value be larger than the input. The compiler verifies both conditions and reports a violation before any code runs. By putting these obligations next to the implementation, developers get immediate feedback instead of debugging a subtle runtime bug.

The benefit is concrete: a contract that would otherwise be expressed in comments or external documentation becomes part of the type-checking pass. The source describes this as “put preconditions, postconditions, and data invariants beside the code they describe.” The result is a single source of truth that the compiler enforces automatically.

## Ownership and borrowed references are checked together with invariants

Evergreen extends the contract idea to memory layout, ownership, and borrowing. The language tracks when a memory plane is live and which references remain valid. A short example from the playground illustrates mutable borrowing:

```rust
let value: usize = 1;
let cell = &mut value;
*cell = 10;
let same = value == 10;
```

The compiler knows that `cell` mutably borrows `value`, that the write through `*cell` updates the original storage, and that the later read of `value` is safe. Because lifetimes are explicit, Evergreen can guarantee that no dangling pointer or data race appears. The site calls this “a compiler that understands memory,” emphasizing that ownership checks are part of the same pass that verifies invariants.

The integration means that a single compilation step validates logical contracts and memory safety. There is no separate static-analysis tool that must be run later; the language’s core type system handles both concerns. This reduces the mental load on developers who would otherwise have to remember two independent rule sets.

## Proofs are erased after verification

Beyond contracts, Evergreen supports lemmas, inductive proofs, and “ideal computations” that exist only for verification. The playground shows a fact that the compiler checks but does not emit in the final binary:

```rust
ideal let expected = integer::from(42);
let value: usize = 42;
fact matches = integer::from(value) == expected;
```

The `ideal` keyword marks a value used solely in proofs, and `fact` declares a proposition the compiler must prove. Once the proof succeeds, the associated code is stripped out, leaving only the executable instructions needed at runtime. The source describes this as “proofs, lemmas by induction, and ideal computations are erased after checking,” meaning the safety guarantees do not affect performance.

Because proofs are erased, developers can write rich specifications without paying a cost in the shipped binary. The language treats verification as a compile-time activity, similar to how a unit test is run during development but not included in production code.

## A concrete workflow in the browser

The Evergreen site offers a WebAssembly-based playground that runs the compiler directly in the browser. Users paste a snippet, press Ctrl / ⌘ + Enter, and see either a successful compilation or a list of contract violations. The interface also lets users download the resulting `.wasm` file, which contains only the executable portion after proof erasure. The page notes that the playground requires JavaScript and WebAssembly, and that the same compiler can be built and run locally for larger projects.

Running the `NonZero` example in the playground demonstrates the full cycle:

1. Write the type with its invariant.
2. Call the constructor with a valid value, the compiler succeeds.
3. Change the argument to `0`, the compiler reports “precondition `x != 0` not satisfied.”
4. Observe that the generated `.wasm` contains no extra code for the invariant check.

This workflow shows how a developer can experiment with contracts, memory safety, and proofs without leaving the browser.

## The takeaway

Evergreen combines explicit contracts, ownership checking, and proof-level verification into a single compilation step. Invariants sit next to types, the compiler enforces them, and any proof code is stripped out before the binary is produced. The practical result is safer systems code that carries no runtime penalty.
